newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World's premier bankers head to Swiss Alps for IMC.
newsitem.headline: World's premier bankers head to Swiss Alps for IMC.

text.p: The world's premier commercial and central bankers will gather in the Swiss Alps next week for the International Monetary Conference (IMC), an annual forum where bankers mix business with pleasure.

Around 130 bankers, representing the world's major banks, and central bank governors from leading nations will meet from June 2-4 in Interlaken, in the shadow of the Jungfrau mountain, to candidly discuss the challenges facing the banking industry.

But it is as an forum for networking on a global scale that distinguishes the IMC -- often described as a financial Davos -- from other conferences and assures the continued attendance of bankers from all over the world.
For financial markets the highlight of IMC is on Wednesday, the third and final day of the conference, when leading central bankers step into the limelight.
But the clash between the German government and Bundesbank over a revaluation of gold reserves could steal the show with Chancellor Helmut Kohl addressing the conference on Monday.
Although the actual business sessions are closed to the press, briefings take place immediately thereafter.

Wednesday's briefing features Alan Greenspan, chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve, Hans Tietmeyer, president of the Bundesbank, Eddie George, governor of the Bank of England and Jean-Claude Trichet, governor of Bank of France.
Yasuo Matsushita, governor of the Bank of Japan, was scheduled to join the briefing, but has cancelled due to debates in Japan's parliament over the reform of Japan's central bank.
Instead, the Bank of Japan will be represented at the IMC by Akira Nagashima, deputy governor.

Other central bankers from the Group of 10 (G10) include Gordon Thiessen, governor Bank of Canada, William McDonough, president of New York Federal Reserve, and Hans Meyer, chairman the Swiss National Bank.

Other central bankers attending include Joseph Yam, chief executive Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Lee Ek Tieng, managing director Monetary Authority of Singapore, Miquel Mancerea, govenor of Mexico's central bank, Hamad Al Sayari, govenor of the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency, Kjell Storvik, governor of Norway's central bank, Bodil Nyboe Andersen, governor of Denmark's central bank and Maurice O'Connell, governor of Ireland's central bank.
Swiss finance minister Kaspar Villiger will address the conference at an informal dinner on Sunday evening.

The idea behind IMC, which held its first meeting in 1954, was to broaden the international knowledge of U.S. bankers. But over the years the IMC's membership has become global and it now consists of 105 member banks, 24 from the U.S. and 81 from outside the U.S.
Its purpose now is to create a better understanding of the international banking and monetary system and key government figures and economic scholars regularly participate.

This year James Wolfensohn, president of the World Bank, Jacques de Larosiere, president of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and Alexandre Lamfallussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, also attend.

The conference will be divided into five closed-door sessions that focus on new banking activities and their risks, the ramifications of Europe's single currency, banking in emerging markets, new roles for regulators, and central banks.

The IMC attracts the top echelon of bankers from around the world with senior officials coming from the U.S., Japan, Germany, China, Canada, Italy, France, Britain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Finland, Australia, Austria, Brazil, Mexico, India, Ireland, Korea, Malaysia, Poland, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Thailand and Switzerland.
